title: The Wise Men of Chelm, the Clocks and the Sunrise
summary: Every clock in Chelm has broken, so the baker bakes at midnight and the rooster crows at noon. What to do? Send Berele the messenger running all night to faraway Zamość, to see when the sun really rises! Through the forest, under the moon, all the way to the sunrise he goes, and on the way back he brings great news for the whole town. A rhyming story based on a folk tale of the Wise Men of Chelm.
pages:
In Chelm there was a clock in every house and every room,
but they had all broken, and each showed a different time — oh, gloom!

The baker baked bread at midnight, the rooster crowed at noon,
and the children walked to school with stars still out, and the moon.
One said "Morning!" and one said "Evening!" — and everyone yawned, so tired and worn.

Reb Shmerel raised a finger: "There's no clock like the sun, and the sun is never wrong,
let's send a messenger to see when it wakes — and how it rises along!"

Berele the messenger, with his long, long legs, set out when it grew dark,
with a stick and a knapsack, one bread roll, and a cheerful, happy spark.
Step-step-step, all night on his feet —
to faraway Zamość, to see the sky and the sunrise sweet!

At night in the forest the owl asked, "Whooo? Whooo?"
And Berele answered, "Me! A messenger from Chelm — and I'm in a hurry, I've no time for you!"
Step-step-step, all night on his feet —
to faraway Zamość, to see the sky and the sunrise sweet!

He hopped from stone to stone across the stream, and sang a song so he wouldn't fall asleep,
and the moon followed him across the sky, peeking at him like a friend, keeping up with each leap.
Step-step-step, all night on his feet —
to faraway Zamość, to see the sky and the sunrise sweet!

When he reached the gate of Zamość, the sky turned orange and gold,
and the sun rose up, round as a cake — "Good morning!" said Berele, and ate his roll, for he was getting hungry, truth be told.

Berele turned right back, with the sun above his head, high in the sky,
he wiped his forehead and dreamed of a glass of water, cool and sweet, his throat so dry.
Step-step-step, all day on his feet —
back from faraway Zamość, with the sun on his shoulders and the heat!

At nightfall Berele reached the gate of Chelm, puffing and glad,
and the town's leaders waited there with lanterns, and faces full of the biggest question they ever had.
"Good news, gentlemen!" Berele cried in a voice of victory:
"In Zamość, the day has just dawned — you see!"

So they set all the clocks to morning, and everyone clapped and cheered,
and the clocks rang out, "Morning!" — while the stars still twinkled, and night hadn't disappeared.

And in the real morning, when the sun rose over the rooftops high,
all the clocks showed the same time — just one, not a minute awry.
And the Chelmites looked at the sun, and at the clocks, and agreed: "No doubt — it's day, we can't deny!"

And Berele slept all day, with a blanket over his shoulders tight,
and in his dream — step-step-step, on his feet all night —
to faraway Zamość, to see the sky and the sunrise bright!
